tasks.title: Predict Row Counts for Different Join Types

description.context: Each join type selects a different region of the Venn diagram between two tables. INNER keeps only the OVERLAP. LEFT keeps everything from the left side, padding right-side columns with null where no match exists. RIGHT mirrors LEFT. FULL OUTER keeps everything from both sides. SEMI is a FILTERING join — it keeps left-side ROWS where a match exists in the right side, and returns ONLY the LEFT-SIDE COLUMNS (no enrichment). ANTI is the inverse of semi — it keeps left-side rows where NO match exists, again with only left-side columns. Semi and anti are filtering tools, not enrichment tools.
description.task: Predict the row count for each join type and recognize what semi returns.
description.validationHint: Draw a Venn diagram: 100 in the overlap, 20 readings-only, 10 meters-only. Each join type selects a different part of this diagram.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: readings: 120 rows, meter_ids M-0001 to M-0120. meters: 110 rows, meter_ids M-0001 to M-0100 plus M-0121 to M-0130. Overlap: 100. Readings-only: 20 (M-0101 to M-0120). Meters-only: 10 (M-0121 to M-0130). No duplicate keys in either side.

fields.label: Inner join (how='inner'): how many rows?
fields.rationale: Inner keeps only the 100 matching meter IDs. 20 readings-only and 10 meters-only are both dropped.

fields.label: Left join (how='left'): how many rows?
fields.rationale: Left preserves all 120 readings. The 100 matched rows get metadata. The 20 unmatched readings get nulls for metadata columns. The 10 meters-only are not included.

fields.label: Full outer join (how='full'): how many rows?
fields.rationale: Full outer keeps everything: 100 matched + 20 readings-only + 10 meters-only = 130.

fields.label: Anti join — readings NOT in meters (how='anti'): how many rows?
fields.rationale: Anti join keeps readings whose meter_id has NO match in meters. M-0101 to M-0120 = 20 readings.

fields.label: A semi join of readings against meters (how='semi') returns how many columns?
options: All 7 combined columns from both tables — semi join is just an inner join with deduplication of the join key.
Only the 4 readings columns — semi join is a FILTER that uses the right table to decide which left rows to keep but does not add right-side columns.
Only the 4 meters columns — semi join keeps the right table's columns because the right table is the 'authority' for membership.
Only the 1 join key column (meter_id) — semi join projects to the join key only as a metadata operation.
fields.correctAnswer: Only the 4 readings columns — semi join is a FILTER that uses the right table to decide which left rows to keep but does not add right-side columns.
fields.rationale: Semi and anti are FILTERING joins, not enrichment joins. They check membership in the right table and emit ONLY left-side columns. Semi keeps left rows that match; anti keeps left rows that do NOT match. The most common Junior confusion is treating semi as 'inner without duplicates'; in reality semi is structurally different — it returns a left-side schema, not a combined schema.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Semi does not enrich; the right table is consulted but not projected.

Option C: Semi keeps the LEFT side's rows and columns; the right is the filter list.

Option D: All left-side columns are kept, not just the key.

description.context: Four join rules drive most production bugs. (1) on='meter_id' merges only the JOIN KEY column. Other columns sharing names (like 'region') are NOT merged — they appear TWICE in the result, creating ambiguity that breaks subsequent col('region') references. (2) Spark's optimizer picks BROADCAST JOIN automatically when one side is below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10 MB). The small side is shipped to every executor, eliminating the shuffle. For larger sides, Spark uses SORT-MERGE or HASH JOIN. (3) Use SEMI for filtering by membership, ANTI for filtering by non-membership; never use inner/left when you only need the left side's rows. (4) Left join row count = LEFT side count when right has unique keys; if right has DUPLICATE join keys, the left rows are multiplied, which is a common silent bug.
description.task: Identify the correct behavior or strategy for each scenario.
description.validationHint: Think about what happens to the column list after each join type, and when Spark broadcasts vs shuffles.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four scenarios from a production code review.

fields.label: Both readings and meters have a 'region' column. After df_readings.join(df_meters, on='meter_id', how='inner'), how many 'region' columns exist in the result?
options: One — the string form on='meter_id' merges ALL shared column names automatically, including 'region'.

Two — on='meter_id' merges ONLY the join key. Other shared column names ('region') remain duplicated, producing two columns named 'region' in the result and causing ambiguity errors on subsequent col('region') references.
Zero — Spark detects the ambiguity and drops both 'region' columns to avoid runtime errors.
One — Spark always keeps only the LEFT table's version of any duplicate column name.
fields.correctAnswer: Two — on='meter_id' merges ONLY the join key. Other shared column names ('region') remain duplicated, producing two columns named 'region' in the result and causing ambiguity errors on subsequent col('region') references.
fields.rationale: The 'on' argument controls only the join CONDITION; it deduplicates only the join key. Non-key shared names are duplicated and you must drop one or rename one before using the column downstream. The most common Junior confusion is assuming Spark 'cleans up' shared names automatically; in reality you must explicitly handle ambiguity (drop the unwanted copy, alias one side, or use df1[c]/df2[c] qualified references).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Only the join key is merged.

Option C: Spark does not auto-drop; it raises errors at use time.

Option D: Both copies are kept; neither is automatically preferred.

fields.label: NordGrid joins 120 rows of readings (120 MB) with 8 rows of substations (1 KB). Which join strategy does Spark use?
options: Shuffle hash join — both sides are hashed and shuffled by the join key, with one side built into a hash table per partition.
Broadcast hash join — the 1 KB substations table is below the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10 MB), so Spark ships it to every executor and joins without shuffling readings.
Sort-merge join — both sides are sorted by the join key on every partition before being merged together.
Nested loop join — every reading row is compared against every substation row in a Cartesian fashion.
fields.correctAnswer: Broadcast hash join — the 1 KB substations table is below the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10 MB), so Spark ships it to every executor and joins without shuffling readings.
fields.rationale: Broadcast joins are Spark's optimization for joining a large table with a small one: the small side is replicated to every executor, eliminating the shuffle cost on the large side. The threshold is configurable (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold). The most common Junior confusion is assuming all joins shuffle; in fact Spark proactively avoids shuffles when one side is small enough to broadcast.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Shuffle joins are used when both sides are too large to broadcast.

Option C: Sort-merge is the fallback for very large joins; broadcast is preferred when possible.

Option D: Nested loop is only used for non-equi joins or as a last resort.

fields.label: An engineer wants to filter readings to only those from active meters. The active meter list is a separate DataFrame. Which join type should they use?
options: Inner join — it correctly filters and adds active-meter columns for completeness.
Left join — it preserves all readings and lets downstream code filter by null.
Semi join — it FILTERS readings by membership in the active list without adding any columns from that list; this is the dedicated tool for membership-based filtering.
Anti join — it returns readings NOT in the active list, which is the inverse of what is needed.
fields.correctAnswer: Semi join — it FILTERS readings by membership in the active list without adding any columns from that list; this is the dedicated tool for membership-based filtering.
fields.rationale: Semi join is the membership-test tool: keep left rows that have a match, return only left columns. Inner would also filter but adds unwanted right-side columns that you would have to drop. The most common Junior confusion is reaching for inner join out of habit; semi expresses 'membership filter' more clearly and avoids accidental column additions.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Inner adds right-side columns the engineer does not want.

Option B: Left does not filter; it preserves all left rows.

Option D: Anti is the inverse — wrong direction.

fields.label: After a left join, the engineer finds 120 rows but expected only 100. What is the most likely cause?
options: The left join added 20 extra rows from the right table; left joins always include right-only rows when the optimizer chooses an outer plan.

The left join preserved 20 LEFT rows that have no match in the right; left always keeps every left row, so unmatched left rows show up with null right-side columns. The engineer expected an INNER join behavior.
The right table has 20 duplicate join keys, multiplying matched left rows by 2 each.
The join condition produced a partial Cartesian product because one side was missing a key column.
fields.correctAnswer: The left join preserved 20 LEFT rows that have no match in the right; left always keeps every left row, so unmatched left rows show up with null right-side columns. The engineer expected an INNER join behavior.
fields.rationale: LEFT preserves every left row by definition. If you got 120 rows but expected 100, you have 20 unmatched left rows with null right-columns. The most common Junior confusion is using left join 'just to be safe' and then being surprised by null-bearing rows; left is the right tool when you genuinely want to KEEP unmatched rows, but inner is the right tool when you want to DROP them.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Left does not include right-only rows; that is full outer.

Option C: Duplicate keys would inflate beyond 120; the row count matches the left side exactly.

Option D: Cartesian products produce row counts in the thousands or millions, not 120.

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Two-Hop Enrichment Pipeline

description.context: NordGrid's Silver enrichment pipeline must join three tables: readings → meters → substations. Readings connect to meters via meter_id. Meters connect to substations via substation_id. The final output must include the reading data, customer_type from meters, and substation_name from substations. All readings must be preserved (use left joins). Both the readings and meters tables have a 'region' column that creates ambiguity after the first join.
description.task: Write a pipeline that: (1) reads all three CSVs; (2) left-joins readings with meters on meter_id; (3) resolves the region ambiguity by dropping the meters table's region column; (4) left-joins the result with substations on substation_id; (5) selects the final columns: meter_id, daily_kw, date, region, customer_type, substation_name; (6) stores the result in a variable called enriched.
description.validationHint: All 120 readings must be preserved. 20 readings will have null customer_type and null substation_name (no meter metadata → no substation link). The final output has 6 columns.

starterScaffold.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName('nordgrid-two-hop-enrichment') \
    .master('local[*]') \
    .config('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', '8') \
    .getOrCreate()

df_readings = spark.read.csv('PS7_data_readings.csv', header=True, inferSchema=True)
df_meters = spark.read.csv('PS7_data_meters_ref.csv', header=True, inferSchema=True)
df_substations = spark.read.csv('PS7_data_substations.csv', header=True, inferSchema=True)

print(f"Readings: {df_readings.count()} rows, columns: {df_readings.columns}")
print(f"Meters: {df_meters.count()} rows, columns: {df_meters.columns}")
print(f"Substations: {df_substations.count()} rows, columns: {df_substations.columns}")

# YOUR SOLUTION BELOW



# YOUR SOLUTION ABOVE

# Verification (do not modify)
print(f"\nEnriched rows: {enriched.count()}")
print(f"Enriched columns: {enriched.columns}")
print(f"Null customer_type: {enriched.filter(col('customer_type').isNull()).count()}")
print(f"Null substation_name: {enriched.filter(col('substation_name').isNull()).count()}")
enriched.show(5)

synthesisNotes.rationale: This is NordGrid's production enrichment pattern: chain two left joins through intermediate reference tables, handle ambiguity, and produce a clean output schema. The null propagation through the join chain is the key insight — 20 readings have no meter match, so their substation_id is null, which means the second join also produces null substation_name. Students must understand that null join keys produce null results in subsequent joins.
